work: Lucretius, De rerum natura I.1–25 (opening), title and first page of a 15th-century humanist manuscript; ex-libris "Amerbachiorum" at the foot.
note: "edition" is the reading from the printed edition supplied with the page, split at the manuscript's own line breaks. Its spelling is the edition's (v, æ, -eis); the scribe writes u for v, e for ae, uses -is endings and many abbreviations (p with a stroke for per/pre, q; for -que, a macron for m/n). The manuscript omits the line "Illecebrisque tuis omnis natura animantum" (I.15 in the edition), so manuscript line 14 is followed directly by "Te sequitur cupide…". "diplomatic" is what the scribe actually wrote, letter by letter; it is filled in only where it has been checked against the image and is otherwise left empty to be completed while tracing.

lines.edition: T. LVCRETII CARI EQ. RO.
POETAE τῶν περὶ τῆς
φύσεως
AENEADVM GENETRIX
HOMINVM DIVVMQVE VOLVPTAS
Alma Venus, cœli subter labentia signa
Quæ mare navigerum, quæ terras frugiferenteis
Concelebras; per te quoniam genus omne animantum
Concipitur, visitque exortum lumina solis:
Te, dea, te fugiunt venti, te nubila cœli,
Adventumque tuum; tibi suaveis dædala tellus
Submittit flores, tibi rident æquora ponti,
Placatumque nitet diffuso lumine cœlum.
Nam simul ac species patefacta est verna diei,
Et reserata viget genitabilis aura Favoni,
Aëriæ primum volucres te, diva, tuumque
Significant initum perculsæ corda tua vi:
Inde feræ pecudes persultant pabula læta,
Et rapidos tranant amneis; ita capta lepore,
Te sequitur cupide, quo quamque inducere pergis:
Denique per maria, ac monteis, fluviosque rapaceis,
Frundiferasque domos avium, camposque virenteis,
Omnibus incutiens blandum per pectora amorem,
Efficis ut cupide generatim sæcla propagent.
Quæ quoniam rerum naturam sola gubernas,
Nec sine te quicquam dias in luminis oras
Exoritur, neque fit lætum, neque amabile quicquam;
Te sociam studeo scribundis versibus esse,
Quos ego de rerum natura pangere conor
